concepts.name: Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) 1948: Framework and Significance
key_dimensions: Classification of industries into four categories: state monopoly, mixed sector, state regulation, and private sector
Role of the state as a facilitator vs. controller — mixed economy foundations laid
Distinction from IPR 1956: why 1948 is considered 'transitional' and 1956 'definitive'
Connection to the broader Nehruvian economic philosophy and the Bombay Plan (1944)

concepts.name: Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) 1956: The 'Economic Constitution' of India
key_dimensions: Three-schedule classification: Schedule A (state monopoly), Schedule B (mixed), Schedule C (private) — specific industries in each
Alignment with the Second Five Year Plan and Mahalanobis model of heavy industrialization
Why IPR 1956 is called the 'Economic Constitution' — its long-lasting regulatory impact until 1991
UPSC trap: industries that were exclusively in Schedule A vs. those that moved between schedules over time

concepts.name: Mahalanobis Model and Its Influence on Industrial Policy
key_dimensions: Two-sector model: emphasis on capital goods (heavy industry) over consumer goods
Rationale: building long-term productive capacity vs. short-term consumption growth
Criticism: neglect of agriculture, small industries, and employment generation
Contrast with Gandhian model (cottage/village industries) and how policy tried to balance both

concepts.name: Industries (Development and Regulation) Act (IDRA), 1951
key_dimensions: Legislative backbone of the 'License Raj': mandatory licensing for specified industries
Provisions for investigation, takeover, and central government control over scheduled industries
Constitutional basis: Entry 52, Union List — Parliament's power over industries of public interest
UPSC trap: IDRA is still in force (not repealed); only the mandatory licensing provisions were progressively removed post-1991

concepts.name: License Raj: Mechanism, Rationale, and Pathologies
key_dimensions: Three-layer control: industrial license + import license + capital goods license
Intended rationale: prevent monopolies, direct investment to priority sectors, balance regional development
Pathologies: rent-seeking, inspector raj, capacity under-utilization, and 'license as entry barrier'
Rajaji's critique and the emergence of Swatantra Party as ideological opposition

concepts.name: MRTP Act, 1969: Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices
key_dimensions: Objective: prevent concentration of economic power and control monopolistic/restrictive trade practices
MRTP Commission: quasi-judicial body — powers and limitations
Threshold-based definition of 'dominant undertaking' (asset limit of Rs. 100 crore) and its arbitrary nature
Replacement by Competition Act, 2002: shift from 'size-based' to 'conduct/behaviour-based' regulation — a critical conceptual difference

concepts.name: FERA vs. FEMA: Regulatory Philosophy Shift
key_dimensions: FERA 1973: criminal law framework, presumption of guilt, exchange control as sovereign right
FEMA 1999: civil law framework, presumption of innocence, facilitation of external trade and payments
Connection to 1991 liberalization and India's BoP crisis — why the shift was inevitable
UPSC trap: FEMA violations are civil offenses; only specific violations (money laundering) attract criminal proceedings under PMLA

concepts.name: New Industrial Policy 1991: Core Provisions and Ideological Shift
key_dimensions: Three pillars: de-licensing, de-reservation, and disinvestment
Reduction of industries requiring compulsory licensing from ~70 to 6 (currently 5: defense, explosives, hazardous chemicals, drugs, aerospace)
Abolition of MRTP pre-entry approval and phased dismantling of public sector reservation
Shift from 'command and control' to 'market and competition' — distinction between liberalization, privatization, and globalization (LPG)

concepts.name: Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs): Evolution of Policy from Expansion to Strategic Disinvestment
key_dimensions: Nehruvian rationale: 'commanding heights of the economy' — why PSUs were privileged
Narasimham Committee and the shift toward disinvestment in the 1990s
Strategic vs. non-strategic classification: 2021 DIPAM policy — four strategic sectors retained with PSU presence
UPSC trap: difference between disinvestment (minority stake sale), privatization (majority + management transfer), and strategic sale — with examples like Air India, BPCL

concepts.name: Small Scale Industries (SSI) Reservation Policy: Intent vs. Outcome
key_dimensions: Items reserved for exclusive SSI production (peaked at 873 items) — rationale of employment and equity
Perverse effects: technology stagnation, inability to achieve economies of scale, fragmentation
Gradual de-reservation post-1997 (Abid Hussain Committee recommendations) and complete phase-out by 2015
Current policy support framework: MSME Development Act 2006, Udyam Registration, and the shift from 'reservation' to 'promotion'

concepts.name: MSME Definition and Its Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Pre-2020 definition based on investment in plant and machinery; post-2020 (Atmanirbhar package) redefinition based on both investment AND turnover
Composite criteria for micro, small, medium — specific thresholds (UPSC favourite for data-based questions)
Significance of upward revision: firms can grow without fear of losing MSME benefits ('graduation problem' addressed)
UPSC trap: service sector MSMEs were treated separately before 2020; now unified definition applies to both manufacturing and services

concepts.name: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Policy Architecture in India
key_dimensions: Automatic route vs. Government approval route: criteria and sectoral allocation
Prohibited sectors for FDI: lottery, gambling, chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business (not construction), tobacco — UPSC trap area
Press Note 3 (2020): FDI from countries sharing land border requires government approval — geopolitical dimension
Consolidated FDI Policy and the role of DPIIT as the nodal agency

concepts.name: Industrial Corridors and the Make in India Strategy
key_dimensions: Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) as the template: smart cities, logistics hubs, integrated manufacturing clusters
National Industrial Corridor Development Programme (NICDP): five corridors and their geographic logic
Make in India (2014): 25 focus sectors, ease of doing business, and FDI facilitation — distinction from Atmanirbhar Bharat
UPSC trap: Make in India is not a scheme with direct financial outlay; it is a policy framework — contrast with PLI which is a financial incentive scheme

concepts.name: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme: Design and Sectoral Coverage
key_dimensions: Core mechanism: incentives based on incremental sales from a base year — 'reward for performance, not capacity creation'
14 sectors covered: mobile phones, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, automobiles, textiles, food processing, etc.
Objectives: import substitution, export promotion, and achieving global scale — connection to 'China+1' strategy
UPSC trap: PLI is different from a subsidy — it is contingent on actual production/sales increment; failure to meet targets means no incentive

concepts.name: Competition Act, 2002 and Competition Commission of India (CCI)
key_dimensions: Three pillars: anti-competitive agreements (Section 3), abuse of dominant position (Section 4), regulation of combinations/mergers (Section 5 & 6)
Shift from MRTP's structure-based approach to conduct-based approach: dominance per se is not illegal, abuse is
CCI as a quasi-judicial regulatory body: suo motu powers, penalty powers (up to 10% of average turnover)
Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023: deal value threshold for merger notification, settlement and commitment mechanism — recent developments

concepts.name: National Manufacturing Policy (NMP) 2011 and Manufacturing in GDP
key_dimensions: Target: increase manufacturing share in GDP to 25% (from ~15%) and create 100 million jobs by 2022 — assessment of achievement
National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs): concept, difference from SEZs
Why India missed the manufacturing ladder: comparison with East Asian developmental states
UPSC trap: NMP 2011 predates Make in India 2014 — both aim at manufacturing but are conceptually distinct policy instruments

concepts.name: Special Economic Zones (SEZs): Policy Evolution and Controversy
key_dimensions: SEZ Act 2005: fiscal incentives (tax holidays), single-window clearance, deemed foreign territory for customs
Boria Mitra Committee and the controversy: land acquisition conflicts, tax revenue loss (MAT applicability), export performance conditionality
Decline of SEZs and emergence of coastal economic zones, industrial townships under DMIC
UPSC trap: SEZs are different from Export Processing Zones (EPZs) — EPZs predate SEZs and had limited domestic area linkages; SEZs allow domestic tariff area (DTA) sales subject to duty

concepts.name: Disinvestment Policy: Instruments, Institutions, and Debates
key_dimensions: Instruments: minority disinvestment, strategic sale, IPO of PSUs, Exchange Traded Funds (CPSE ETF, Bharat-22 ETF)
Institutional evolution: Disinvestment Ministry → Department of Disinvestment → DIPAM (Department of Investment and Public Asset Management)
National Investment Fund (NIF): where disinvestment proceeds go and their earmarked use
UPSC trap: disinvestment receipts are capital receipts, not revenue receipts — they reduce fiscal deficit but are a one-time asset sale, not sustainable revenue

concepts.name: Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) Reforms and the Jan Vishwas Act
key_dimensions: World Bank's Doing Business Report parameters: India's rank improvement from 142 (2014) to 63 (2020) — and discontinuation of the report
Key reforms: IBC 2016, GST, single-window clearance, decriminalization of minor offenses
Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023: decriminalization of 183 provisions across 42 Acts — converting imprisonment to fines
UPSC trap: discontinuation of World Bank's Doing Business Report (2021) due to data integrity concerns — India now relies on Business Reform Action Plan (BRAP) rankings by DPIIT

concepts.name: Atmanirbhar Bharat and the New Definition of Self-Reliance
key_dimensions: Five pillars: economy, infrastructure, technology-driven system, vibrant demography, demand
Distinction from import substitution industrialization (ISI) of the 1950s–70s: Atmanirbhar aims at global competitiveness, not autarky
Policy instruments under the umbrella: PLI, defence indigenization (negative import lists), National Education Policy, one district one product
UPSC trap: Atmanirbhar Bharat is a vision/framework, not a single scheme — multiple ministries operate schemes under this umbrella, often leading to confusion in attribution
